newsitem.title: UK: Asian oil deliveries jump 20 percent - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Asian oil deliveries jump 20 percent - analysts.

text.p: Asian oil deliveries have risen by more than 20 percent so far this year as local refiners boosted capacity and oil producers jockeyed to secure market share, oil analysts said on Monday.
The hefty gain reflects the growing trend of major producers looking east to Asia's exploding energy needs as a way to expand their core customer lists.

Total year-to-date crude oil deliveries to destinations East of Suez jumped by some 2.5 million barrels a day (bpd) from the fourth quarter 1996, with a similar gain also noted for mid-March shipments over year-ago figures, according to tanker tracker Oil Movements.

"While the increase of flows east over December incorporate a seasonal element, the 2.5 million bpd year-on-year gain is a good indicator of Asian refiners' growing reliance on longer-haul barrels," said consultant Roy Mason at Oil Movements.
Crude oil deliveries East of Suez were estimated to be on the order of 13.8 million bpd, versus an estimated 11.3 million bpd during the same period last year.
"This figure includes the majority of movements of West African sweets to Asia, along with an uptick in shipments out of the Arabian Gulf," Mason said.

Big vessel shipments eastward out of the Arab Gulf and the Red Sea combined increased by some 600,000 bpd during the first two months of 1997 compared to the same period a year ago, according to London-based shipping consultant Charles Lawrie of Richardson Lawrie.

"Virtually all of the gains out of the Arab Gulf were eastbound," Lawrie said. Increases of large vessel fixings out of the AG and Red Sea ports were pegged at 670,000 bpd for eastbound and westbound voyages combined.

Asian refiners have looked further afield for crude supplies due in part to tightening sulphur specifications across the region, analysts said. A lack of the requisite refinery sophistication has meant a greater reliance on lower sulphur sweet grades, which has also pushed Asian refiners towards West African producers when regional sweet availability is scarce or prices to high.
Profitable shipping economics can also enhance the West Africa to Asia play.
"One specific factor driving increased West African flows east is the affordability of freight into India," said Mark Jenkins, director of research at tanker broker Simpson, Spence & Young.
India takes some 28 percent of reported eastbound fixings out of West Africa.
"The proximity of India to the Arab Gulf eradicates the bulk of backhaul costs seen in other long-haul voyages," Jenkins said.
SS&Y estimates West African flows east to have climbed five percent in this year's first quarter over a year ago, to some 855,000 bpd.

In the near term, at least 12 million barrels from Nigeria, Angola, Cameroon, and Equatorial Guinea are expected to load in the first 10 days of April for refineries in South Korea, China, and India, even as the region enters heavy seasonal maintenance, traders said.
Trans-Pacific shipments of Alaskan North Slope grade into Asia represent another factor behind upped East of Suez arrivals.
"We've been sending about 100,000 to 120,000 bpd to Asia out of Valdez," said one British Petroleum crude analyst.
That represents nearly a tenth of total ANS production levels, and a 60,000 to 80,000 bpd gain over levels seen last summer.
